topic: Supreme Court of India II — mixed tiers
description: Articles 124-147, jurisdiction types, collegium, basic structure, key landmark cases

questions.stem: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on:
questions.explanation: Supreme Court — inaugurated on 28 January 1950 (two days after the Constitution came into force). Replaced the Federal Court of India (set up 1937 under the Government of India Act 1935) and the Privy Council (London). First sitting at the Chamber of Princes, Parliament House. Moved to its present building (Tilak Marg, Delhi) in 1958. First Chief Justice — H.J. Kania. Building shape — symbolic of scales of justice. Apex court of India; final court of appeal. Articles 124-147 deal with the Supreme Court.

questions.stem: The current sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court of India (judges including the CJI) is:

options.option_text: 34 (CJI + 33 other judges; raised from 31 by amendment in 2019)

questions.explanation: Initial strength (1950) was 8 (CJI + 7), raised to 11 (1956), 14 (1960), 18 (1978), 26 (1986), 31 (2009), 34 (2019). Current — 34 judges (1 CJI + 33). The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019 raised it from 31 to 34. Article 124(1) — Constitution provides for the Supreme Court 'consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges'. Parliament is empowered to fix the number by law.

questions.stem: The 'collegium system' for appointment of judges is:

options.option_text: A judge-led process evolved through SC judgments — Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998)

questions.explanation: Collegium — not a constitutional body; evolved through SC interpretations of Article 124 + 217: First Judges Case (1981) — Centre dominant. Second Judges Case (1993) — judiciary primacy; collegium of CJI + 2 senior-most judges. Third Judges Case (1998) — collegium expanded to CJI + 4 senior-most for SC appointments. NJAC (National Judicial Appointments Commission) — 99th CAA (2014) tried to replace collegium with a 6-member commission (3 judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent persons); STRUCK DOWN by SC in 2015 (4-1 majority, 4th Judges Case) on 'basic structure' grounds (judicial independence). Collegium remains the operative mechanism, but is widely criticised for opacity. Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) — governs the process.

questions.stem: The 'basic structure doctrine', that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 is not absolute, was laid down by the Supreme Court in:

options.option_text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), 13-judge Bench, 7-6 majority

questions.explanation: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) — landmark; 13-judge bench (largest ever); 7-6 majority. Held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution INCLUDING Fundamental Rights, but CANNOT alter the BASIC STRUCTURE of the Constitution. Basic features (illustrative, evolved over time): supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, democracy, judicial review, free + fair elections. Earlier cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) — Parliament can amend FRs; Golaknath (1967) — Parliament cannot amend FRs (overruled by 24th CAA). Minerva Mills (1980) — reaffirmed basic structure; struck down 42nd CAA's attempt to give Parliament unlimited amending power.

questions.stem: The 'curative petition' before the Supreme Court was conceptualised in which case to allow correction of judgments after the dismissal of a review petition?

options.option_text: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)

questions.explanation: Curative petition — last resort after a review petition is dismissed. Conceptualised in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002). Grounds: (1) violation of natural justice; (2) bias of a judge that came to light later. Heard by a bench of 3 senior-most judges (with the original judges if available). Examples of high-profile curative petitions: Nirbhaya case (rejected — death penalties confirmed); Bhopal Gas victims; Sahara case; recent same-sex marriage curative (rejected). Vishaka — laid down sexual harassment guidelines (later replaced by POSH Act 2013). Maneka Gandhi — expanded Article 21 (procedure must be fair, just, reasonable). Indra Sawhney — 27% OBC reservation, 50% cap.

questions.stem: Article 32 of the Constitution provides for the:

options.option_text: Right to constitutional remedies (writs) — moving the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights

questions.explanation: Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies. Empowers individuals to move the Supreme Court directly when their FRs are violated. Dr B.R. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Five Writs (also available under Article 226 to High Courts): (1) HABEAS CORPUS — produce the body (against illegal detention); (2) MANDAMUS — we command (to compel a public official to perform duty); (3) PROHIBITION — bars a lower court from acting beyond jurisdiction; (4) CERTIORARI — to be informed (quash an order of a lower court); (5) QUO WARRANTO — by what authority (challenge appointment to a public office). HC jurisdiction (Art 226) is wider — also for legal rights, not only FRs.

questions.stem: The retirement age of a Judge of the Supreme Court of India is:
questions.explanation: Retirement: SC Judge — 65 years (Article 124(2) proviso). HC Judge — 62 years (Article 217). District Judge — 60 years (varies; service rules). UPSC member — 65 years. CAG — 65 years. Election Commissioners — 65 years. Salary of judges — fixed by Parliament; charged on Consolidated Fund of India (cannot be voted on); cannot be reduced after appointment except during a financial emergency. Removal — only by impeachment (Article 124(4)) on grounds of 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity'; needs 2/3 majority of present-and-voting + absolute majority of total strength in EACH House. No SC judge has been impeached so far (V. Ramaswami, 1993, narrowly survived in Lok Sabha after Congress abstained).
